# Diagnosing a Single-Key Immobilizer Failure on a 2007 Honda Fit

When one of two keys stops working on a vehicle that previously operated flawlessly, the distinction between a mechanical failure and an electronic security lockout is critical. In the case of the 2007 Honda Fit described, the symptoms point away from a standard immobilizer system failure and toward a specific transponder communication issue.

The user reports that while both keys function mechanically, one key illuminates the green dashboard light upon insertion but fails to start the engine. The second key operates normally. This behavior explicitly rules out a global immobilizer malfunction. If the immobilizer control unit (ICU) had lost its ability to communicate with the ECU or if the system were completely disabled, neither key would allow the starter relay to engage. The fact that the dashboard light activates confirms that the ignition switch is receiving power and the vehicle's central processing unit is acknowledging the physical presence of a key.

The core issue lies in the handshake protocol between the transponder chip embedded in the key fob and the vehicle's immobilizer receiver. Modern Honda vehicles utilize a rolling code system where the ECU validates the digital signature sent by the transponder before permitting fuel injection and spark. When only one key fails to start the car, it suggests that the specific transponder inside that key has either ceased broadcasting or is broadcasting an invalid ID that the ICU rejects after a single attempt.

### Transponder Chip Failure vs. Battery Issues

A common misconception is that this scenario involves a dead battery in the remote entry fob. It is important to distinguish between the two functions of a Honda Fit key: the passive transponder chip and the active remote control circuitry. The green light on the dashboard confirms the passive system is being detected; however, if the immobilizer logic interprets the signal as invalid, it will block ignition regardless of whether the remote locking/unlocking function still works (if that were to be tested separately).

However, in many 2007 model year units, the transponder chip and the remote control circuitry share a single battery compartment. If the battery voltage has dropped significantly, the active RF transmitter may fail while the passive induction loop remains functional enough to trigger the green light, yet insufficient to maintain a stable digital handshake with the ECU.

To verify this without purchasing new keys immediately, the most direct diagnostic step is to swap the batteries between the two key fobs. If the key that currently fails starts working after the battery swap, and the previously good key fails, the root cause was simply depleted cell voltage affecting the transponder's communication range or signal integrity.

### The ICU and ECU Handshake Logic

If swapping the batteries resolves the issue, the diagnosis is complete. However, if the first key remains dead even with a fresh battery, the transponder chip itself may have degraded or been damaged by moisture ingress or physical impact. Unlike a mechanical lock cylinder where pins simply wear out, the RFID coil and antenna within the steering column can also suffer from corrosion or connection issues over time.

In this specific scenario, since only one key is affected, replacing the immobilizer control unit (ICU) is generally unnecessary and economically inefficient. The system requires the ICU to fail completely to reject both keys simultaneously. The trade-off here involves cost versus complexity: attempting to program a new aftermarket chip into the existing fob is often unreliable on older Honda architectures due to proprietary rolling code algorithms that require dealer-level diagnostic tools to synchronize.

The most reliable path forward, given that one key functions perfectly as a reference, is to replace the battery in the faulty key first. If that fails, the only viable technical solution without specialized programming equipment is to have the vehicle dealership or a qualified locksmith program a new transponder ID into a replacement fob, utilizing the working key as the master source for cloning the identity.

Attempting to bypass the immobilizer by cutting the ignition coil wires or disabling the ICU wiring is a last resort that voids warranties and introduces safety risks regarding anti-theft protocols. The green light serves as the system's explicit warning that the digital signature check failed, and respecting that signal ensures you are addressing the correct component rather than fighting the security logic of the vehicle.
